title: Fighting Illicit Cigarette Trade in the Americas
gist: PMI's Latin America and Canada president cites a KPMG study that nearly one in three cigarettes in the region is illicit ($8.5 billion tax revenue lost in 2025) and argues for sensible regulation plus enforcement rather than bans and tax hikes. This is an industry-authored advocacy piece.

insights.claim: KPMG's first regional study finds nearly one in three cigarettes consumed in Latin America and Canada is illicit, the highest rate in the world.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Illicit share erodes legal-market volume and excise revenue for listed tobacco companies.
insights.locator: In April, at an event organized by

insights.claim: About $8.5 billion of tax revenue was lost in 2025 across the 11 countries studied, with about 77 billion illicit cigarettes consumed.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Fiscal motivation for governments to prioritize enforcement.

insights.claim: Illicit consumption fell less than total cigarette consumption, as consumers shift from legal to illicit products.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Legal volumes are decline faster than total smoking, which hurts legal operators.

insights.claim: Illicit cigarettes make up 89% of consumption in Panama and 84% in Ecuador, and Brazil is the largest illicit market with over 40 billion cigarettes in 2025.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Country-level exposure map for legal tobacco sales.
insights.locator: The scale of the problem is striking

insights.claim: Consumer product bans have created illicit markets in virtually every case, and overregulation and taxation paired with weak enforcement push legal markets underground; Brazil's e-cigarette ban created a growing illicit market without ending underage use.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Industry thesis against bans, relevant for vape-regulation outcomes.
insights.quote: Consumer product bans have created illicit markets in virtually every case.

insights.claim: Australia's extreme regulation has contributed to a market in which more than 80% of nicotine products come from illicit trade, with gang fights over the black market.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Used as cautionary example by the industry; self-interested source.

insights.claim: In countries where illicit trade is already widespread, further tax increases or bans on smoke-free products will not curb underage use, illicit trade or smoking.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Signals PMI lobbying positions on excise and smoke-free product rules.

insights.claim: Transnational organized crime networks have diversified into illicit trade, using control of strategic routes to smuggle goods beyond customs reach, and Interpol links illicit trade to trafficking, corruption and money laundering.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Illicit trade is a financing stream for organized crime.

insights.claim: 42% of PMI revenue now comes from smoke-free products, up from 2.7% ten years ago, and the company says it is committed to ending cigarette sales in the future.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
insights.so_what: Company-stated mix shift; note it is author's own marketing claim.

insights.claim: A study in Preventive Medicine Reports estimates nearly one-fifth of adolescents in Latin America reported using e-cigarettes.
insights.speaker: CAN KUTERDEM
